strengths: SpatialVID addresses a useful data gap by combining real-world videos with estimated camera poses, depth, dynamic masks, structured captions, and motion instructions. Its reported 2.71 million clips and 7,089 hours represent a substantial curation effort.

The pipeline is practically motivated: motion-oriented collection, quality filtering, dynamic-scene reconstruction, and pose-conditioned caption refinement form a coherent approach to producing spatial supervision at scale.

The manuscript documents substantial scene and motion diversity and provides a 1,146-hour HQ subset with more balanced motion categories. These resources could support camera-controlled generation and spatial learning without requiring a new model architecture.
weaknesses: The central claim of high-quality spatial annotations lacks independent quantitative validation. Figure 6 compares predicted trajectories without reference trajectories, pose errors, or timing measurements. No representative accuracy audit is reported for depth, dynamic masks, or motion instructions. Smooth trajectories can still be geometrically incorrect, so acceleration filtering does not establish annotation accuracy. The annotations are model estimates, and the manuscript's framing around geometric ground truth overstates their evidential status.

No downstream training experiment establishes the claimed improvements in model generalization or performance. Section 4 reports distributions and examples, rather than reconstruction, motion understanding, or controllable-generation results. For a dataset contribution, benchmark superiority is unnecessary, but the absence of both independent annotation validation and demonstrated downstream utility leaves its principal scientific claims insufficiently supported.

The caption-refinement contribution is supported mainly by an illustrative correction in Figure 9 and caption-length statistics. There is no systematic comparison of motion accuracy before and after refinement or assessment of hallucination. Figure 14 also contains a concrete inconsistency: the shopping-street Motion Trends include left translation, while its camera description states that there are no lateral shifts.

The Panda70M comparison does not establish general quality superiority. SpatialVID is selected using the same quality and motion properties subsequently plotted in Figure 13; narrower distributions and more camera movement primarily demonstrate the intended selection. Reconstruction failure on Panda70M is not independently shown to result from insufficient motion. Comparisons with closer spatial datasets are limited to descriptive metadata.

Reproducibility and accessibility are insufficiently specified for a dataset-centered submission. The manuscript provides no dataset access or release protocol, licensing information, source-level train/test partitioning, or deduplication procedure. Important implementation details are also missing, including motion-label thresholds, smoothing settings, acceleration rejection criteria, HQ sampling thresholds, caption prompts, and pose serialization conventions.

The claimed coverage of real-world dynamics requires qualification. Section 3.1 explicitly excludes videos dominated by moving objects, substantial blur, severe occlusions, or difficult camera optics. This sensible reconstruction-oriented selection favors tractable camera motion, but limits the evidence for usefulness in complex dynamic interactions. Overall, the scale and integrated annotations are worthwhile merits, while the unresolved accuracy and utility questions determine the weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: SpatialVID addresses a relevant data gap by combining camera poses, depth, dynamic masks, structured captions, and motion instructions for real-world videos. The reported 2.71 million clips and 7,089 hours represent a substantial curation effort.

The pipeline offers a practical integration of existing tools: motion-focused collection, quality filtering, MegaSaM-based geometry, SAM2 mask refinement, and pose-informed captioning. This combination has potential value for camera-controlled generation and spatial learning without requiring a new reconstruction algorithm.

The manuscript provides useful collection statistics, explicit thresholds for several filters, computational costs, and qualitative annotation examples. The 1,146-hour HQ subset also attempts to reduce motion-category imbalance.
weaknesses: The central claim of high-quality spatial supervision lacks independent validation. Section 3.3 and Figure 6 provide selected trajectory visualizations without reference trajectories, numerical pose/depth errors, or measured runtime comparisons. Neither the depth-model replacements nor SAM2 refinement receive quantitative evaluation. These are estimated annotations, not independently established geometric ground truth; trajectory smoothness alone cannot establish correctness.

No downstream training experiment supports the abstract's claim of improved generalization and performance. Section 4 contains descriptive statistics and a Panda70M comparison, but no reconstruction, motion-understanding, or camera-controlled generation results. A dataset need not achieve state-of-the-art performance, but the absence of both annotation-quality measurements and demonstrated training utility leaves its principal scientific value insufficiently substantiated.

The comparison in Figure 13 largely measures properties already targeted by collection and filtering. Narrower luminance distributions, greater movement, and more trajectory turns do not independently establish superior annotation quality. MegaSaM reconstruction failure also does not by itself establish that Panda70M clips lack motion. Comparable annotation-quality evidence against spatial datasets such as DynPose100K or Sekai is absent.

Caption accuracy is not evaluated through a human audit or a motion-label benchmark. Caption lengths and word frequencies cannot validate spatial correctness. Moreover, Figure 9 describes panning while the refined text describes translation, and Figure 14's shopping-street motion tags include left translation while its camera description explicitly denies lateral shifts. These examples raise concrete concerns about consistency across annotation fields.

Reproducibility and accessibility are insufficiently specified for a dataset contribution. The manuscript provides no dataset access or release procedure, licensing information, source-level train/test splits, or deduplication protocol. Important implementation details are also missing, including motion and acceleration thresholds, smoothing parameters, HQ sampling rules, caption prompts, and geometric annotation sampling frequency.

The broad dynamic-scene claims require qualification: Section 3.1 explicitly excludes videos dominated by moving objects and other difficult reconstruction conditions. This is a reasonable curation choice, but the resulting bias toward smooth, reconstructable footage limits the claimed coverage. Overall, the substantial collection effort favors recognizing the work's merits, while the unresolved validation and reproducibility gaps determine the weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: SpatialVID addresses a useful data gap: large-scale real-world videos combining camera poses, depth, dynamic masks, structured captions, and motion instructions. The reported 2.71 million clips spanning 7,089 hours represent a substantial curation effort with potential value for reconstruction and camera-controlled video generation.

The pipeline integrates sensible components: motion-oriented collection, explicit quality filtering, dynamic-scene reconstruction, SAM2-based mask refinement, and pose-conditioned caption refinement. Several filtering thresholds, annotation models, and computational costs are documented.
The 1,146-hour HQ subset explicitly addresses imbalanced scene and motion distributions. The statistics and qualitative examples demonstrate coverage of multiple environments and camera trajectories.
weaknesses: The decisive concern is that annotation reliability—the central value of this dataset—is not independently established. There are no quantitative pose/depth accuracy measurements, mask evaluations, or representative human audits of captions and motion instructions. Figure 6 shows predicted trajectories without reference trajectories or numerical timing results, so it cannot substantiate the claimed accuracy–speed advantage. Smoothness filtering also cannot establish geometric correctness. These are estimated annotations, not independently verified ground truth.

The abstract claims improved model generalization and performance, but the manuscript contains no downstream training or evaluation experiment. The dataset contribution need not achieve state-of-the-art results, but without either strong annotation validation or a controlled utility experiment, its claimed benefits remain insufficiently supported.

The Panda70M comparison in Section 4.3 mainly measures properties used to select SpatialVID itself. More concentrated luminance distributions and larger motion statistics do not independently demonstrate better supervision. Comparisons with relevant spatial datasets are largely descriptive, and the depth-model upgrades, mask refinement, and pose-conditioned captioning receive no quantitative ablations.

Important reproducibility details are missing: geometric annotation sampling rate and scale conventions, acceleration rejection thresholds, motion-label thresholds and smoothing parameters, caption prompts and pose encoding, and the precise HQ sampling procedure. No dataset access mechanism, licensing information, or source-separated evaluation splits are specified, leaving practical reuse and leakage control unclear.

The scope of the dynamic-scene claim needs qualification. Section 3.1 explicitly excludes videos dominated by moving foreground objects and other difficult reconstruction conditions. This is reasonable curation, but dynamic-object prevalence and performance across difficulty levels are not quantified, limiting evidence for general dynamic-scene coverage.

There are additional presentation inconsistencies: Figure 11 claims increased caption lengths whereas Section 4.2 reports reduced motion-caption length; Figure 9 describes a pan while the refined text describes translation; and Figure 14 includes a left-translation tag alongside a description asserting no lateral shifts. These are secondary to the validation gaps but weaken confidence in the claimed semantic consistency.
